title: Open Source in the Age of AI: More Important Than Ever
text:
Every few years, something comes along that makes the question of open vs. closed feel urgent in a new way. Right now, that thing is AI and specifically, the large models that are reshaping how software gets written, how decisions get made, and how information gets filtered.
The stakes of openness have never been higher.
Here’s the tension: the most capable AI systems today are mostly closed. The weights aren’t public. The training data isn’t disclosed. The reasoning process is opaque even to the people running them. You interact with these systems through an API, and you take on faith that they’re doing what you think they’re doing.
That’s a significant amount of trust to extend to any system, let alone one that’s increasingly embedded in consequential decisions.

title: Open Source in the Age of AI: More Important Than Ever
text:
Why Openness Matters
Open source AI doesn’t solve everything. Open weights don’t guarantee interpretability. Releasing a model doesn’t automatically tell you what it was trained on or what biases it inherited. Openness is necessary but not sufficient. But it’s still necessary.
When a model’s weights are public, researchers can study it. When training code is available, problems can be reproduced and debugged. When the community can audit rather than just observe, accountability has somewhere to land. We’ve seen this play out already. Some of the most important findings about how large language models behave — how they fail, what they’re sensitive to, what they’re quietly optimising for — have come from researchers who could actually get inside the thing. That kind of scrutiny is only possible when something is open.

title: Open Source in the Age of AI: More Important Than Ever
text:
The Concentration Question
There’s also the concentration question. Closed AI systems tend to centralise power. A handful of companies control the most capable models, which means they control a growing share of what’s technically possible. Open source is one of the few mechanisms we have to counteract that — to ensure that capability doesn’t become permanently gated behind a small number of commercial relationships.

title: Open Source in the Age of AI: More Important Than Ever
text:
The Path Forward
I’m not naive about this. Building frontier AI is genuinely expensive. There are real reasons organisations don’t open-source everything. But the direction matters, and the pressure matters. The open source community pushing for transparency, reproducibility, and accessible models is doing important work — not just for software idealists, but for everyone who’ll eventually be on the receiving end of these systems. We spent decades building an open web and then watched it slowly close. I’d rather not repeat that with AI. The time to care about openness is before it’s gone.

title: Notes from Carnegie Mellon: Probability, PDEs, and the Future of Research
text:
Earlier this month, I had the opportunity to attend the Summer School on Topics at the Interface of Probability and PDEs at Carnegie Mellon University. The program brought together graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and faculty interested in the rich interactions between probability theory and partial differential equations.
As a statistics PhD student, I was initially drawn by the mathematics. The lectures exposed us to modern research problems where probabilistic methods and PDE techniques complement each other in surprising ways. Yet one of the most memorable parts of the experience came not from a theorem or proof, but from a career discussion that forced me to think more deeply about research itself.


One statement from the career talk stayed with me:

Good mathematics is interpretable, structured, and interconnected.

In a world increasingly driven by artificial intelligence, there is a temptation to optimize for speed alone. We can now obtain explanations, code, and even proofs faster than ever before. Yet speed without understanding can be dangerous.
The speaker emphasized the importance of balancing our own thought process with the convenience of AI tools. Rather than outsourcing thinking entirely, we should use these tools to amplify understanding. The goal is not merely to arrive at answers, but to build mental models that connect ideas across fields.
Perhaps that is what makes mathematics enduring: its ability to reveal structure beneath complexity.



Another observation was both simple and provocative.
For many years, degrees have often served as signals of intelligence or persistence. Increasingly, however, the market appears to be shifting toward practicality. The question will become less about credentials and more about capability.
Who can solve meaningful problems?
Who can produce high-quality work efficiently?
Who can adapt and learn quickly?
The value of expertise will remain, but its demonstration may look different than it has in the past.



One question I continuously wrestle with is:

How do you choose good research problems?

The discussion offered a practical framework.


Interesting problems often emerge through conversation. Different researchers see different gaps, frustrations, and opportunities. Listening carefully can reveal questions that would never appear in a textbook.



Research does not happen only at a desk covered in papers.
The suggestion was to intentionally create time for brainstorming—whether through solitary reflection, conversations with colleagues, or even structured sessions with AI tools. Creativity deserves a place on the calendar.



Do not stop at understanding that a proof works.
Ask yourself:

What is the key idea?
How would I explain it to someone else?
How would I have discovered this argument myself?

The deeper understanding often lies beneath the technical details.




The speaker described strong researchers as possessing a combination of seemingly contradictory traits:

Obsessive enough to pursue difficult questions for long periods.
Open-minded enough to abandon assumptions when evidence points elsewhere.

This resonated with me.
Many of the opportunities that have shaped my academic journey came from pursuing interests deeply rather than broadly. Excellence often requires sustained attention.
One piece of advice for the transition from PhD to postdoctoral research was particularly refreshing:

Do research. Don’t worry.

Worry creates noise. Research requires focus.
When we spend too much energy on uncertainty, we lose energy for discovery. The challenge is not eliminating uncertainty but learning to work despite it.



As I reflected on the week, I realized that several of these ideas connect to notes I have kept for years.
I maintain a catalog of research ideas, questions, and curiosities. Some are half-formed. Some may never become projects. Yet the advice from the summer school reminded me that important problems do not disappear simply because they are difficult. Sometimes they need time.
Most importantly, I left Carnegie Mellon with a renewed conviction:
If I enjoy what I am doing, and I have the opportunity to pursue it, then I should focus and do it.
Research is difficult. Mathematics is difficult. Building expertise is difficult.
But there is a special kind of joy in diving deeply into something that genuinely fascinates you.
For me, that may have been the most valuable lesson of the week.

title: About
text:
I believe that numbers tell stories — sometimes quietly, sometimes in ways that surprise us.
I’m fascinated by how data can reveal patterns that help us understand people, systems, and possibilities.
Most days, I’m working on problems that live at the edge of statistics, machine learning, and communication — figuring out how to make insights feel human again.

Now
I’m currently a PhD student in Statistics, exploring how modern methods in optimization and experimental design can make real-world decisions smarter and more efficient.
Along the way, I’m learning to translate complex statistical ideas into stories that inspire — whether that’s through writing, teaching, or building tools that help others see data differently.


Previously
Before diving deep into research, I spent time studying the foundations of data science, learning how numbers shape narratives, and building small projects that blend analytics with creativity.
That mix of art and analysis is something I still carry into everything I do.
